title: THEY WERE CRYING FOR A FALSE GOD… WHILE STANDING AT THE DOOR OF THE TRUE ONE
paragraphs: THEY WERE CRYING FOR A FALSE GOD… WHILE STANDING AT THE DOOR OF THE TRUE ONE

The disturbing vision of women weeping for Tammuz in Ezekiel 8 reveals a terrifying possibility: You can stand near the presence of God, carry the appearance of devotion, and still give your deepest love to something that cannot save you.
There is something deeply unsettling about the sound of someone crying outside a door.
Especially when the One behind that door has the power to heal everything they are crying about.
Imagine standing at the entrance of God's Temple in Jerusalem.

The walls have witnessed generations of prayers. The sacred courts have heard the cries of repentant sinners. This is the place associated with the name of the LORD, the God who delivered Israel from slavery, sustained them in the wilderness, and repeatedly called His people back when they wandered.
But something is terribly wrong.
Women are sitting near the entrance.
They are weeping.
Their tears are real. Their grief is visible. Their devotion is unmistakable.
But their tears are not being offered to the LORD.
They are weeping for Tammuz.
And the God whose Temple they have approached is showing His prophet something horrifying.
Not every tear is an act of worship.
Not every spiritual experience is evidence of surrender.
And not everything that makes your heart tremble is worthy of your heart.
Before you dismiss this as an ancient story about people who worshiped strange gods, consider something.
What if the most frightening part of Ezekiel's vision is not how different those worshipers were from us?
What if it is how painfully familiar their misplaced devotion can become?
Because sometimes the thing standing between us and God is not something we openly hate.
Sometimes it is something we love more than Him.
And that is where this story begins to reach into places we would rather keep hidden.
The prophet Ezekiel was living among the Judean exiles in Babylon when the LORD gave him an extraordinary vision.

According to Ezekiel 8:1, it was the sixth year of the exile, in the sixth month, on the fifth day. Ezekiel was sitting in his house with the elders of Judah before him when the hand of the Sovereign LORD came upon him.
In the vision, the Spirit lifted him and brought him to Jerusalem.
What he was about to see would expose the spiritual corruption that had taken root among God's covenant people.
This was not a casual tour of the Temple.
It was a revelation of covenant betrayal.

Ezekiel first saw an idolatrous image provoking jealousy. Then he was shown elders burning incense before images of creeping things and detestable idols. Later, he would see men turning their backs toward the Temple of the LORD and bowing toward the rising sun.
And between these scenes came one of the strangest and most haunting statements in the entire book.
Ezekiel 8:14 records:
"וְהִנֵּה־שָׁם הַנָּשִׁים יֹשְׁבוֹת מְבַכּוֹת אֶת־הַתַּמּוּז"
Ve-hinneh sham ha-nashim yoshvot mevakkot et-ha-Tammuz.
A close translation of the Hebrew is:
"And behold, there the women were sitting, weeping for Tammuz."
The Hebrew word מְבַכּוֹת (mevakkot) comes from the verb בכה (bakhah), meaning "to weep" or "to cry."
The form describes the women as engaged in weeping.
And the name תַּמּוּז (Tammuz) identifies the object of their lament.
That matters.
The text does not say these women were crying out to the LORD in repentance.
It does not say they were grieving over the sins of Jerusalem.
It says they were weeping for Tammuz.
Then the LORD said to Ezekiel:
"Have you seen this, O son of man? You will see still greater abominations than these." — Ezekiel 8:15, ESV
Imagine hearing those words.
God was not impressed by the intensity of their religious emotion.
He was exposing the object of their worship.
And that distinction can change the way we examine our own hearts.

Tammuz was associated with Dumuzi, a deity known from ancient Mesopotamian religious traditions. In those traditions, Dumuzi was connected with fertility, vegetation, shepherding, and seasonal cycles. Ancient laments mourned his loss or descent into the realm of the dead.

The precise ritual being practiced by the women in Ezekiel's vision is not explained in detail by Scripture. Scholars generally understand the scene as reflecting a mourning practice associated with this deity.
We should not invent details the Bible does not give us.
Scripture does not tell us the women's names, their personal histories, or the private thoughts behind their tears.
But it tells us enough to understand the offense.
A practice associated with another deity had entered the sacred precincts of the LORD's Temple.
The place that should have testified to the exclusive worship of Israel's God had become a setting for religious compromise.
And here is the tragedy.
They were near the Temple.
But nearness to a holy place did not make their worship holy.
They were expressing deep emotion.
But the depth of their emotion did not make its direction right.
They were participating in a religious practice.
But religious activity could not transform an idol into the living God.
That is a warning we desperately need.
Because we live in a world that often treats sincerity as the highest form of truth.
"If it feels right, follow it."
"If it makes you happy, it must be good."
"If your heart is deeply moved, surely God must be pleased."
But Scripture challenges that assumption.
You can sincerely believe something false.
You can passionately pursue something destructive.
You can cry over something that is quietly becoming your master.
And you can mistake the strength of your feelings for the approval of God.
That does not mean tears are wrong.
Jesus Himself wept.
John 11:35 gives us those two extraordinary words:
"Jesus wept."
Our Savior was not ashamed of human grief.
He entered it.
He understood it.
He carried it.
The problem in Ezekiel 8 was not that women were crying. Nor was it that women, rather than men, were uniquely guilty. The surrounding vision condemns the idolatry of both male and female worshipers.
The problem was the worship of a false god within the place devoted to the LORD.
And the same danger can confront any human heart.
You may never have heard of Tammuz before today.
You may never have bowed before a carved image.
You may never have participated in an ancient mourning ritual.
But have you ever given something created the kind of ultimate trust, devotion, or obedience that belongs to the Creator?
Have you ever been more terrified of losing someone's approval than of disobeying God?
Have you ever protected a sinful relationship because you could not imagine living without it?
Have you ever compromised your convictions to preserve your reputation?
Have you ever pursued money so desperately that your peace disappeared whenever your bank account changed?
Have you ever known that God was calling you to surrender something, but kept negotiating with Him because you were not ready to let it go?
This is where the ancient Temple begins to feel uncomfortably close.
Because an idol does not always announce itself as an idol.
Sometimes it arrives as a dream.
Sometimes as romance.
Sometimes as ambition.
Sometimes as comfort.
Sometimes as the desperate need to be admired.
Sometimes even as a religious platform that becomes more important to us than the Christ we claim to proclaim.
A good gift becomes spiritually dangerous when we begin demanding from it what only God can give.
A relationship can be a blessing without becoming our savior.
Work can be meaningful without becoming our identity.
Money can be useful without becoming our security.
Ministry can be fruitful without becoming our god.
And this is the question Ezekiel's vision forces upon us:
What are you giving your deepest devotion to while telling yourself that God still has first place?
That question hurts because many of us know how to maintain an appearance.
We know how to say, "God is good," while privately resisting His correction.
We know how to post Bible verses while carrying bitterness we refuse to release.
We know how to lift our hands during worship while holding tightly to something Christ has commanded us to surrender.
We know how to speak about faith while secretly building our entire sense of worth on human applause.
And perhaps the most painful truth is this:
Sometimes we are not unaware of the compromise.
We are simply exhausted from trying to justify it.
We tell ourselves it is not that serious.
We compare ourselves with someone whose sin looks worse.
We promise God we will change later.
We call conviction "guilt" and try to silence it.
We ask for peace while refusing to abandon the very thing disturbing our souls.
But God loves His people too much to pretend that divided worship is harmless.
The LORD's jealousy in Scripture is not petty insecurity. It is His holy opposition to covenant unfaithfulness and to the false worship that destroys His people.
In Exodus 20:3, He commands:
"You shall have no other gods before me."
Not because He is one option competing for our attention.
But because He alone is God.
And nothing else can bear the weight of our worship.
Think about the idols people build their lives around.
They promise fulfillment but demand endless sacrifice.
They promise acceptance but make us terrified of rejection.
They promise control but leave us anxious about everything we cannot control.
They promise identity but collapse the moment circumstances change.
They promise freedom but slowly teach us to obey our appetites.
And when they fail us, we often run back to them, hoping they will finally give what they have never been able to provide.
That is the cruelty of idolatry.
It asks for the devotion of a god while possessing none of God's power to save.
But Ezekiel's vision does not end with the women weeping.
And the story of God's people does not end with the exposure of their sin.
This is where the Gospel begins to shine against a very dark background.
Because the same prophetic book that reveals the corruption of the human heart also announces God's promise to transform it.
Later, in Ezekiel 36:26, the LORD declares:
"And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you." — ESV
In Hebrew, the promise begins:
"וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב חָדָשׁ"
Ve-natatti lakhem lev chadash.
"And I will give you a new heart."
Notice what God promises.
Not merely improved religious behavior.
Not merely a more convincing outward appearance.
Not merely stronger emotions during worship.
A new heart.
A transformed inner life.
A work of grace reaching deeper than performance.
Ezekiel 36:27 continues with God's promise to put His Spirit within His people and move them to walk in His statutes.
That is the difference between merely hiding an idol and receiving a heart that increasingly loves the living God.
And Christians recognize the fulfillment of God's saving promises through Jesus Christ and the gift of the Holy Spirit.
Jesus did not come merely to make religious people more religious.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile rebels to God.
He came to bear the judgment that sin deserves and bring forgiveness through His death and resurrection.
He came to do what idols never could.
He came to give life.
And perhaps you need to hear this more than anything else today.
The God who exposes your idols is also the God who calls you to return.
His Word may uncover something you have spent years hiding.
His truth may challenge a relationship you have defended.
His holiness may confront the secret compromises you have learned to tolerate.
But the invitation of the Gospel is not to despair.
It is to repent and believe.
Repentance is more than feeling terrible about what we have done.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) refers to repentance, a turning of mind and life toward God.
Biblical repentance involves acknowledging sin, turning away from it, and returning to the LORD in faith.
It is not purchasing forgiveness through tears.
It is not earning grace through self-punishment.
It is not promising to become perfect before approaching Christ.
It is coming to the Savior because we cannot save ourselves.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — ESV
Read that again.
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because the sacrifice of Jesus Christ is sufficient.
This is what makes the Gospel so astonishing.
The idols we serve demand that we give ourselves to them.
But Jesus gave Himself for sinners.
The idols we trust cannot forgive our rebellion.
But Jesus shed His blood for the forgiveness of sins.
The idols we chase cannot conquer death.
But Jesus rose from the grave.
The idols we cling to eventually fail.
But Christ remains faithful.
And there is another detail in Ezekiel that should leave us trembling.
In Ezekiel 8, the people were corrupting the Temple associated with God's dwelling among His covenant people.
But in John 2:19–21, Jesus speaks of the Temple in a way His disciples later understand as referring to His own body.
He says:
"Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." — John 2:19, ESV
John explains that Jesus was speaking about the Temple of His body.
Do you see the extraordinary movement of the biblical story?
Ezekiel reveals the horror of idolatry in God's Temple.
The Gospel reveals the Son of God giving His own body to death and rising again so sinners can be reconciled to God.
This does not mean the women weeping for Tammuz were secretly reenacting the death and resurrection of Christ. Scripture does not teach that, and we should not force such a connection.
The contrast is far more powerful when we allow the text to speak truthfully.
Tammuz belonged to the religious traditions of the ancient world.
Jesus Christ entered real human history, was crucified under Pontius Pilate, and was proclaimed risen by His witnesses.
Christian faith does not rest on a seasonal fertility ritual.
It rests on the saving work of the crucified and risen Lord.
And He is not asking you to manufacture religious emotion to impress Him.
He calls you to trust Him.
To follow Him.
To surrender the throne of your heart.
Because the greatest tragedy is not simply that human beings sometimes worship false gods.
It is that we can become so attached to those false gods that we resist the mercy of the true One.
Maybe your idol is not obvious to anyone else.
Maybe it is the person you cannot stop chasing even though the relationship keeps pulling you away from obedience.
Maybe it is the success you have sacrificed your integrity to obtain.
Maybe it is the resentment you have carried for so long that forgiveness now feels like surrendering your identity.
Maybe it is the secret habit that keeps promising relief while leaving you ashamed.
Maybe it is your own image.
The version of yourself you desperately need everyone to admire.
The version that never struggles.
Never doubts.
Never confesses.
Never needs help.
And perhaps you have become so skilled at appearing strong that you have forgotten how to be honest before God.
But listen.
Jesus already knows.
He knows the thought you would never post.
He knows the compromise you keep explaining away.
He knows the prayer you stopped praying because you were afraid of what obedience might cost.
He knows the disappointment that hardened into anger.
He knows the wound you keep covering with spiritual language.
And still, His Gospel calls sinners to come.
Not because He approves of the darkness.
But because He alone can bring us out of it.
In Matthew 11:28, Jesus says:
"Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." — ESV
Not come to the idol that keeps exhausting you.
Not come to the applause that disappears tomorrow.
Not come to the relationship that has become your entire reason for living.
Come to Me.
There is a kind of exhaustion that sleep cannot fix.
It is the exhaustion of living divided.
Trying to serve Christ while protecting the thing that competes with Him.
Trying to experience peace while resisting the truth.
Trying to look whole while privately falling apart.
And sometimes the beginning of healing is a painfully simple confession:
"Lord, I have loved something more than I have loved You."
No excuses.
No performance.
No bargaining.
Just truth.
And a willingness to turn toward Jesus.
Perhaps your prayer tonight needs to be this:

"Father, show me what has taken Your rightful place in my heart. Expose what I have defended. Forgive what I have hidden. Teach me to love what You love and turn away from what dishonors You. I cannot change my own heart by sheer determination. I need Your mercy. I need Your Spirit. I need Jesus. Lead me into genuine repentance and faithful obedience. In Christ's name, amen."
There is no shame in bringing your sin into the light of Christ.
The danger is insisting that darkness is where you belong.
And if this article has uncovered something in your life, please do not rush past that moment.
You do not need to share every private struggle publicly. Some matters are best brought to God and to a trusted, mature believer who can walk with you.
But you do not have to keep pretending that the battle does not exist.
Someone reading silently may need to know that genuine change through Christ is possible.
Your story may not be finished.
But God's grace is not exhausted.
There may also be someone in your family, your church, or your circle of friends who needs this message.
Not because you want to embarrass them.
Not because you have appointed yourself their judge.
But because you love them enough to remind them that Jesus is better than anything that competes for their soul.
Because a message like this should not end with a moment of emotion.
It should lead us back to the Word of God.
Back to prayer.
Back to obedience.
Back to the local church.
Back to the cross.
Back to Jesus.
And if Gospel Warrior has been a source of biblical encouragement in your life, I want to invite you to consider something beyond reading and sharing.
Not as a payment for God's favor.
Not as proof that your faith is genuine.
But voluntary support can be a meaningful expression of Christian generosity when it is given freely, wisely, and for the right reasons.
The apostle Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
That is the spirit in which we invite you.

Some believers may prayerfully choose to make that support part of their planned Christian giving. Others may rightly prioritize their local church, family responsibilities, and other needs. Traditional tithes and offerings should not be confused with a required payment to an online ministry.
What matters is not pressure.
It is faithful stewardship and a willing heart.
The products are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
The resources are not the Savior.
Jesus is.
The Gospel is already the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, as Romans 1:16 declares.
But your generosity can help carry that message farther.
Imagine someone scrolling through Facebook late at night.
Someone exhausted from pretending.
Someone quietly trapped in a sin they are afraid to confess.
Someone convinced they have gone too far to return.
Someone whose faith has become little more than an outward routine.
And then they see an article you shared.
They read about women weeping for Tammuz at the entrance to God's Temple.
They begin examining the misplaced devotion in their own heart.
They remember that Christ died for sinners.
They open their Bible.
They pray honestly for the first time in months.
They seek help.
They begin to turn toward Jesus.
You may never know that happened.
But it is one reason sharing truth with compassion matters.
I want you to think about the entrance to that Temple.
The women sitting there.
The tears falling.
The religious devotion directed toward a god who could not save.
And I want you to remember that the living God was not blind to what was happening.
He saw.
He spoke.
He exposed.
And through the unfolding testimony of Scripture, He revealed His saving mercy in Jesus Christ.
Now imagine your own heart standing in the light of that truth.
No religious performance.
No carefully edited image.
No excuses.
Just you before the God who knows everything.
What would He find occupying the place that belongs to Him?
And what would happen if, today, you finally surrendered it?
You do not need to manufacture a dramatic moment.
You do not need to prove the sincerity of your repentance through public emotion.
You need the Savior.
The One who died.
The One who rose.
The One who calls sinners to repent and believe.
The One who forgives.
The One who transforms.
The One who is worthy of everything.
Because the true tragedy of Ezekiel 8 is not that people were weeping.
It is that they were giving their devotion to something that was not God.
And the hope of the Gospel is that our story does not have to end there.
You can turn.
You can confess.
You can come to Christ.
And by His grace, you can learn to love Him above everything else.
The most heartbreaking thing is not to be found weeping at the door of God's house, but to spend your life clinging to what cannot save you while the Savior calls you to come home.
